corrected_value.title: Skilled musicians are not subject to the McGurk effect

decisions.quote: Overall, the findings of Proverbio and colleagues [ 2 ] seem indeterminate: they are consistent with the presence of a McGurk effect for musicians and they are also consistent with the absence of such an effect. For these reasons, it is valuable to conduct a close replication of this study to assess whether skilled musicians really are not subject to the McGurk effect.
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding identify Reference 2 (Proverbio et al., 2016, Sci. Rep. 6, 30423, doi:10.1038/srep30423, 'Skilled musicians are not subject to the McGurk effect') as the sole original study re-tested by this replication.

decisions.quote: This article reports a pre-registered, higher-power replication of that study (using twice the sample size and changing from a between- to a within-participants manipulation). Contrary to the original study's conclusion, we find that musicians do show a large and statistically significant McGurk effect and that their effect is no smaller than that of non-musicians.
decisions.reason: The authors explicitly conclude that their results refute the original study's conclusion that skilled musicians are not subject to the McGurk effect, finding instead a large, statistically significant McGurk effect in musicians in both the replication analysis and targeted analysis. Although the Discussion notes that the original study's noisy, underpowered estimates had wide confidence intervals compatible with a positive effect, the authors' overall replication verdict is that the original substantive conclusion is contradicted and ruled out.

decisions.quote: This article reports a pre-registered, higher-power replication of that study (using twice the sample size and changing from a between- to a within-participants manipulation).
decisions.reason: The study collects new experimental data from 62 skilled musicians and 62 non-musicians to re-test the published finding of Proverbio et al. (2016). Incidental commentary on reporting inconsistencies in the original paper's summary tables does not alter the record type from replication.
